These emissions have increased by nearly a thousandfold since the 1970s and are concentrated in densely populated urban areas, driven by the rapid expansion of sludge incineration, codisposal, and composting. Our findings reveal a cross-media pollution transfer embedded in sustainability transitions and call for sludge disposal to be incorporated into UNEP mercury budget and Minamata Convention assessments.

title: The purinergic receptor P2Y13 controls the activation and mode of division of adult ventricular–subventricular zone neural stem cells
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
The ventricular–subventricular zone (V-SVZ) is the most active germinal area in the mammalian brain and it continues to generate newborn neurons throughout life. This area harbors a population of neural stem cells (NSCs) that exist in different states of activation: quiescent NSCs, primed NSCs, and activated NSCs. There are currently few specific markers to effectively discern each state. Likewise, the molecular signals that control the transition from quiescence to activation remain largely unexplored, and the factors that controls whether dividing NSCs differentiate or self-renew are poorly understood. Here, we present evidence that the metabotropic P2Y
                    13
                    purinergic receptor plays a critical role in regulating adult neurogenesis. We found that P2Y
                    13
                    is specifically expressed in NSCs within the adult V-SVZ and that its levels can be used to distinguish quiescent from activated NSCs. P2Y
                    13
                    signaling promotes NSC activation, enhancing lineage progression as opposed to their self-renewal. Conversely, pharmacological blockade or genetic silencing of P2Y
                    13
                    receptors favors NSC quiescence. Thus, we consider the metabotropic P2Y
                    13
                    purinergic receptor a pivotal modulator of NSC dynamics.

title: Multifunctional multiphysics metamaterials via decomposition-based multiobjective optimization design
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Metamaterials offer unprecedented control over physical fields through their microstructure, but current design methods cannot meet the demands of scenarios involving active sources, multiphysics field coupling, and multifunctional requirements. Moreover, existing approaches are generally developed for specific functions, making it difficult to integrate different functionalities and select the functional priorities within a single structure. To overcome these limitations, this study presents a systematic inverse design framework for multifunctional multiphysics metamaterials via multiobjective optimization. To uniformly explore the Pareto front, which clearly exhibits trade-offs among functionalities and facilitates the selection of functional priorities, we employ dynamic normalization into the decomposition-based multiobjective evolutionary algorithm. A robust anisotropic unit-cell database is constructed and used for generating metamaterials with optimized microstructures for multifunctionality. Three complex cases are studied that can simultaneously achieve mechanical cloaking plus stress minimization, thermal cloaking plus stress minimization, and direct current cloaking plus thermal stress minimization. Furthermore, the proposed framework is employed in potential engineering problems, for example, to realize mechanical cloaking by embedding functional components in structural materials, while minimizing the surrounding stress on functional components for mechanical protection when the assembled structures are compressed, thereby decoupling the interaction between functional and structural components. This systematic framework expands the capabilities of metamaterials in complex multiphysics coupling, offering a robust blueprint for future intelligent, structurally and functionally integrated systems.

title: USP46 restrains K63-linked polyubiquitination–dependent aggregation and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in lupus nephritis
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: The activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome necessitates its aggregation within the dispersed trans-Golgi network (dTGN) and subsequent transport from the dTGN to the microtubule organizing center (MTOC), a process facilitated by HDAC6. However, the regulatory mechanisms governing the formation of NLRP3 aggregates remain insufficiently understood. In this study, we demonstrate that proteasome impairment induces polyubiquitination and aggregation of NLRP3 at the MTOC. We demonstrate ubiquitin-specific protease 46 (USP46) as a key factor that recognizes NLRP3 as a substrate and restricts nondegradative K63-linked polyubiquitination at lysine residue K930, thereby preventing excessive aggregation, transport to the MTOC, and inflammasome activation. Furthermore, myeloid-specific knockout of USP46 exacerbates renal injury and inflammation in both lipopolysaccharide-induced-induced endotoxic shock and pristane-induced lupus nephritis models. Our findings provide insights into the regulatory mechanisms underlying the aggresomal activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome.

title: A tetravalent bispecific protein enables targeted degradation of VCAM-1 and VEGFR for treatment of choroidal neovascularization
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a leading cause of irreversible vision loss, is driven by pathological choroidal neovascularization (CNV). Although anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapies remain the clinical standard, their utility is constrained by incomplete responses in nearly 50% of patients and off-target risks—such as geographic atrophy—stemming from non-specific VEGF blockade. Here, we identify a robust correlation between vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1) and VEGF/VEGF receptor (VEGFR) expression in aqueous humor from AMD patients and in murine CNV models. Thus, we engineered a tetravalent bispecific protein, RHV, by functionalizing an L-rhamnulose-1-phosphate aldolase scaffold with peptides that selectively bind VCAM-1 and the VEGFR on neovessels. The tetravalent design confers high apparent affinity, enhancing pathological endothelial targeting while sparing healthy retinal vasculature. RHV induces concurrent internalization and lysosomal degradation of both VCAM-1 and VEGFR via a head-to-tail binding mode, leading to sustained inhibition of the VEGF/VEGFR, PI3K/AKT and Apelin/APJ signaling pathways. In murine CNV models, a single intravitreal injection of RHV exhibits superior ocular retention and lesion penetration, achieving therapeutic efficacy comparable to aflibercept [a ligand-trap fusion protein for VEGF-A, VEGF-B and placental growth factor (PIGF)] at one-quarter of the molar dose. This dual-receptor degradation-based strategy represents a targeted and durable approach for treating ocular neovascularization.

title: An aggregation-prone region in talin controls talin self-interactions and regulates integrin adhesion complex dynamics
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Talin is a mechanosensitive scaffold that couples integrins to the actin cytoskeleton and coordinates signaling at integrin adhesion complexes. A second integrin-binding site (IBS2) has been proposed within the R11–R12 region of the talin rod, although the molecular basis of this interaction has remained unclear. Here, we show that talin R11 contains a cryptic aggregation-prone region (APR) embedded within Helix50. Mechanical unfolding of R11 exposes this motif, enabling high-affinity talin–talin interactions and force-dependent self-association. The isolated APR forms amyloid-like fibers in vitro, and APR-disrupting gatekeeper mutations suppress fiber formation, talin self-association, and cellular recruitment. We therefore designate this motif Aggregation-Prone Region 1 (APR1). Mitochondrial-targeting experiments demonstrate that APR1-dependent recruitment occurs in cells independently of focal adhesions and integrins. APR1 overlaps the vinculin-binding site in Helix50, and vinculin disrupts preexisting talin assemblies, revealing a mechano-chaperone function for vinculin. Disruption of APR1-mediated self-association does not impair adhesion formation but instead generates larger, more talin-rich adhesions with altered assembly dynamics and signaling properties, indicating a role for APR1 in regulating adhesion remodeling. Together, these findings identify force-dependent talin self-association as a mechanism in mechanotransduction and suggest that the region previously designated IBS2 functions primarily as an aggregation-prone regulatory element.

title: Intrinsically motivated humans and agents in open-world exploration
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
What drives exploration? Understanding the intrinsic motivation to explore is a long-standing challenge in both cognitive science and AI. In this study, we directly compare adults, children aged 8 to 12 y, and AI agents exploring a complex, open-ended environment called Crafter (
                    1
                    ). We study how three common information-theoretic intrinsic objectives—entropy, information gain, and empowerment—relate to their behavior. We find that all three are positively correlated with human exploration progress for both children and adults, although entropy and empowerment are more strongly related to exploration progress in children than information gain. Furthermore, across agents and humans we observe that entropy initially increases rapidly, then plateaus, while empowerment increases continuously, suggesting that in early exploration they look for novel states, while in advanced exploration they look for states they can control. Finally, we find preliminary evidence that private speech about goals may aid exploration in children. Our data are available at
                    https://github.com/alyd/humans_in_crafter_data
                    .

title: Maize genetic diversity is largely unstructured by human ethnolinguistic diversity in its center of origin
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Population structure and environmental features often capture major axes of genetic variation in many species. Yet the impacts of human activity often remain unquantified. For domesticated species that rely on human activity for survival and dispersal, human movements and cultural differences may play key roles patterning genetic diversity. Maize is a staple crop of enormous cultural importance to indigenous peoples of the Americas, but cannot survive or disperse without farmers. Using publicly available genotyping and passport data from approximately 2,000 traditional maize varieties, more than 500 whole genome sequences of humans from Mexico, and indigenous linguistic maps, we quantify anthropogenic effects on maize genetic diversity in the Americas. Maize shows very little overall structure, highlighting the effectiveness of indigenous farmers in moving and mixing maize populations. While principal components of maize diversity show meaningful correlations to human genetic diversity, our linear modeling suggests little additional impact of human population structure beyond shared geography. Though differences in maize diversity are often patterned by language locally, we find only weak genome-wide effects at larger spatial scales. Despite the relatively weak global signal of anthropogenic effects, linguistic Genome-wide association, outlier

title: On-going retinal neuronal degeneration despite clinical stability in glaucoma
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Glaucoma, a leading cause of irreversible blindness, involves progressive retinal ganglion cell loss. Early detection of this neurodegeneration is critical, yet current clinical methods often identify disease only after substantial damage has occurred. This preliminary study used high-resolution adaptive optics–optical coherence tomography (AO-OCT) to track individual retinal ganglion cells in patients and healthy volunteers over 3 to 5 years. Results revealed higher neurodegeneration in glaucoma compared to normal aging. We observed 4.16 to 6.86% annual decrease in cell density in glaucoma, far exceeding the 0.27% cell loss rate observed in the healthy volunteer group. Critically, AO-OCT detected progression significantly earlier, identifying cell loss 0.74 years before conventional OCT and 1.49 years before visual field testing. These findings demonstrate AO-OCT as a more sensitive tool capable of monitoring glaucomatous damage with superior precision, potentially representing a major advancement over current clinical imaging.

title: Oxygen-mediated projection microstereolithography for sub–100-μm zirconia dental veneers
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: High-resolution vat photopolymerization of ceramics is constrained by light scattering, which broadens cured features, and by shallow penetration, which limits interlayer bonding. This trade-off is particularly damaging for microscale structures such as no-preparation dental veneers. We introduce an oxygen-mediated projection microstereolithography strategy in which an oxygen-permeable release film creates an interfacial inhibition field in high-solid–loading zirconia slurry. Rather than uniformly reducing curing, oxygen preferentially filters low-dose scattered light at pattern edges while preserving curing in the projected core. This anisotropic inhibition reshapes the accuracy-depth trade-off, enabling optimized multilayer printing of thin-wall zirconia. The process enabled reproducible fabrication of ∼80-micrometer zirconia veneers with high trueness, improved marginal adaptation, and handling-related strength comparable to substantially thicker milled veneers. The approach provides the potential for minimally invasive dental restoration and a general strategy for high-resolution additive manufacturing of strongly scattering ceramic suspensions.

title: Local translational program at the muscle-tendon junction endows domain identity in muscle syncytia
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: How cells establish specialized subdomains is a fundamental question in cell and tissue biology. Skeletal muscle fibers, among the largest cells in the body, are multinucleated and form distinct regions such as the neuromuscular and myotendinous junctions (MTJs), the latter forming a critical interface between muscle and tendon that transmits contractile force. While transcriptional heterogeneity among myonuclei has been described, whether local translation contributes to domain identity remains unknown, largely due to the lack of tools for domain-specific manipulation. Here, we introduce MTJ-AAV, a viral system that enables selective genetic targeting of MTJ myonuclei. This approach allowed MTJ-specific ribosome tagging and revealed extensive translational regulation underlying MTJ biology and its remodeling during exercise. Untranslated regions of these transcripts were sufficient to control regionalized translation. Notably, the Krüpper-like factor–family transcription factors emerged as translationally up-regulated targets at the MTJ, where they drive local gene expression. Our findings establish local translation as a key layer of subcellular specialization and provide a versatile toolkit for dissecting spatial molecular regulation within muscle syncytia.

title: Entropic tightening of knots in granular chains under vibration
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Knots are common in long chains, from DNA and proteins to everyday strings, yet direct observation of knot dynamics is difficult. Using granular chains on vibrating platforms, we directly visualize knot dynamics and find that knot cores spontaneously tighten, a behavior observed across different knot types. We quantitatively explain spontaneous knot tightening using knot-tube theory: segments confined within the knot core experience entropic loss and tend to escape the core to gain conformational entropy. Although driven granular chains are not in thermodynamic equilibrium, their steady-state knot-size statistics are approximately captured by equilibrium statistical mechanics and Monte Carlo simulations. Analyses of state-transition probabilities and time-reversal asymmetry suggest a weak violation of detailed balance when the granular dynamics are projected onto the knot-size coordinate. Finally, we discuss the possible relevance of knot tightening to topoisomerase-mediated DNA unknotting.

title: A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease progression
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Identifying the neurobiological basis of cognitive vulnerability is essential for preventing Alzheimer’s disease (AD). We derived the Alzheimer’s Resilience-Vulnerability Connectome (ARC) by contrasting SuperAgers (SA), an extreme phenotype of preserved late-life memory, with AD using resting-state fMRI. ARC distinguished SA from AD in a discovery cohort (
                    N
                     = 290; AUC = 0.85) and replicated independently (
                    N
                     = 143), involving prefrontal, temporal, and insular networks and associating with brain age. Applied to cognitively unimpaired adults (discovery:
                    N
                     = 818; replication:
                    N
                     = 497), ARC-based subtyping revealed SA-like and AD-like subgroups with comparable baseline cognition but divergent longitudinal trajectories. AD-like individuals exhibited faster cognitive decline, greater amyloid-β accumulation, and higher AD conversion risk. Exploratory GWAS nominated
                    CLYBL
                    and
                    FRMD6
                    as candidate novel loci associated with the subtype difference. These findings suggest that ARC captures a continuous connectomic dimension of cognitive aging spanning SA, cognitively typical aging, and AD, highlighting the potential of functional connectomic variation for early risk stratification in AD.

title: Clinically derived micro- and nanoplastic uptake drives spatiotemporally confined metabolic stress revealed by bond-selective imaging
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Although microplastics and nanoplastics (MPs/NPs) are pervasive environmental contaminants, our understanding of cellular toxicity remains incomplete, as adverse effects are often attributed to long-term intracellular accumulation, while the spatiotemporal onset of cellular damage remains poorly defined. Here, we use chemical bond–selective stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy and cell models that decouple continuous exposure from intracellular retention to directly visualize clinically derived MP/NP-cell interactions. Cellular stress occurs primarily during MP/NP exposure, accompanied by alterations in lipid droplet (LD) composition. In contrast, following extracellular removal, intracellularly retained MP/NP become largely inert, with recovery of lipid metabolism and cellular functions. Lipidomics identifies arachidonic acid (AA) as a key dysregulated metabolite, and SRS imaging further reveals transient, spatially confined AA enrichment in MP/NP–proximal LDs during uptake. Phospholipid coating of MP/NP attenuates LD alterations and cytotoxicity while preserving particle internalization, establishing uptake-driven metabolic stress, rather than long-term intracellular retention, as a primary source of MP/NP–induced damage.

title: Stony coral symbioses show variable responses to future ocean conditions
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Coral reefs support over a quarter of marine species and nearly a billion people worldwide but are also among the ecosystems most threatened by anthropogenic impacts. There is long-standing debate about whether coral symbioses will be disrupted or respond adaptively under future ocean conditions. Using a factorial 2.5-year future-ocean mesocosm experiment across eight coral species representing the major coral lineages, we tracked symbiont community shifts within replicate fragments from the same individual coral. Some corals exhibited stochastic divergence, whereas others showed deterministic shifts in symbiont community composition. Heat stress generally reduced symbiont diversity and promoted predictable restructuring, consistent with deterministic adaptation to moderate thermal stress but stochastic accumulation of diversity under extreme conditions. We propose that adaptive and stochastic responses represent endpoints along a continuum of host-orchestrated symbiont sorting. This study bridges coral reef ecology with broader host-microbiome theory, offering an integrated perspective on how symbiotic systems may respond to environmental change.

title: Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Mars is reputed to lack ongoing volcanic activity. However, marsquakes were revealed recently, and clues to volcanism younger than tens of million years have accumulated. While sulfur dioxide, so far undetected, could testify to ongoing eruptive activity, evidence of active magma chambers may be better identified by seepage of halogen gases, such as hydrogen chloride (HCl). Observations by Atmospheric Chemistry Suite led to the widespread observations of HCl at part-per-billion levels in the atmosphere of Mars during the warm perihelion period, attributed to aerosol-atmospheric sources. Here, we report HCl detections during the cold aphelion season that are isolated in the Alba Mons region. We also identify fresh and narrow (<1 meter) fissures in this area, which we interpret to be potential HCl pathways rooted into magmatic bodies at depth. Our results are best explained by ongoing igneous processes in the Martian interior.

title: Cooper’s Ferry/Nipéhe, stratigraphic integrity, and confirming early inland dispersal: Evaluating peopling of the Americas modeling
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Statistical models shape debates over the timing and geography of the initial peopling of the Americas, but their value depends on testing their assumptions against archaeological evidence. We examine the Apparent Stratigraphic Integrity Index (ASI), used to infer postdepositional mixing at Late Pleistocene sites and support a relatively late occupation of temperate North America. ASI describes vertical discontinuity in binned artifact-frequency profiles; it does not directly measure artifact movement or stratigraphic integrity. At Cooper’s Ferry/Nipéhe, Idaho, the 5-centimeter absolute-elevation bins used to calculate ASI do not reflect the actual stratigraphic positions of artifacts across the irregular LU2 surface on which LU3 loess accumulated. The resulting ASI value cannot support claims of large-scale vertical mixing. Independent chronological, stratigraphic, pedogenic, archaeological, and excavation evidence supports the integrity of the ∼16,000–calibrated-years-before-the-present occupation. Cooper’s Ferry/Nipéhe provides early inland evidence expected under coastal-migration models, showing that models should be evaluated against archaeological evidence rather than used to override it.

title: BCLAF1 links RNA splicing to ATF4-dependent metabolic adaptation in acute myeloid leukemia
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is driven by genetic alterations and non-mutational mechanisms that disrupt normal hematopoiesis and support leukemic cell survival. While the mutational landscape of AML is well characterized, the non-genetic processes sustaining leukemic maintenance remain less understood. Using human AML cells and murine models, we identify BCL2-associated transcription factor 1 (BCLAF1) as a key regulator of leukemic progression through control of mRNA processing. BCLAF1 physically associates with core spliceosome components and regulates alternative splicing programs in leukemic cells. Mechanistically, BCLAF1 is required for productive splicing of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) mRNA, thereby sustaining ATF4 protein levels and downstream metabolic gene expression programs. Loss of BCLAF1 reduces ATF4 levels, leading to impaired de novo amino acid biosynthesis and increased sensitivity to venetoclax. Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism linking RNA splicing control to metabolic adaptation in AML, identifying BCLAF1 as a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

title: Amphipathic helices repurpose a Patched/NPC1-like cholesterol transporter to function at Plasmodium–erythrocyte membrane contact sites
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
The interface between the malaria parasite
                    Plasmodium spp.
                    and its host erythrocyte critically mediates nutrient uptake, lipid exchange, and protein export required for parasite replication and thus pathogenesis. Approximately half of this interface consists of narrow membrane contact sites, a region defined by only 3 to 4 nm of aqueous space between the parasite plasma membrane and the parasitophorous vacuole membrane. Despite its extent, the region remains largely uncharacterized and inaccessible, not least due to its narrowness. The sole identified resident is the
                    Plasmodium falciparum
                    Niemann-Pick Type C1-Related protein, PfNCR1, an essential Patched/NPC1-like cholesterol transporter, suggesting this conserved transporter family has evolved an unconventional adaptation for localizing to membrane contact sites that can reveal a mechanism to access the region. Here, using live-cell microscopy and assessment of cholesterol homeostasis, we identify a helix–linker–helix (HLH) domain as the necessary modification for efficient PfNCR1 localization. We find that correct localization is required for the parasite to maintain low cholesterol levels, connecting targeting to function. Using a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored fluorescent reporter as a minimal membrane-associated protein, we show that the HLH domain is sufficient to drive localization to the narrow membrane contact site region. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that targeting depends on the physicochemical character of the targeting domain rather than a specific primary sequence, identifying amphipathicity as a determining property of the HLH domain. Taken together, we propose physicochemical partitioning as a fundamental principle for protein targeting at the
                    Plasmodium
                    –erythrocyte interface, and for driving direct functional interactions of a Patched/NPC1-like protein with a second membrane.

title: A DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein–Arp complex–CAPZA3 scaffold is essential for perinuclear theca assembly and fertilization
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Fertilization is a fundamental biological process that enables the fusion of a spermatozoon with an oocyte to initiate embryonic development. However, the underlying mechanisms leading to fertilization failure remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrated that the actin-related protein (Arp) family members ACTRT2 and ACTRT3 are essential for fertilization in both humans and mice, whereas ACTL10 is dispensable for fertility and the human-specific ACTL8 may play a role in early spermatogenesis. Ultrastructural and immunofluorescence analyses revealed that, during spermatogenesis, ACTRT2 or ACTRT3 deficiency disrupts the assembly of subacrosomal layer of the perinuclear theca (SAL-PT), leading to acrosome detachment and subsequent manchette abnormalities, which in turn impairs the formation of the postacrosomal sheath of the PT. These structural defects were accompanied by reduced abundance of the candidate sperm-borne oocyte-activating factors PAWP and PLCζ. Moreover, knockout of
                    Actrt2
                    or
                    Actrt3
                    severely impaired spermatozoa’s ability to penetrate the zona pellucida during in vitro fertilization. Mechanistically, ACTRT2, ACTRT3, ACTL7A, ACTL7B, and ACTL9 form a testis-enriched Arp complex in the SAL-PT and maintain the stability of one another. This complex interacts with the PT protein CAPZA3, which subsequently binds and stabilizes PLCζ. Additionally, the Arp complex interacts with DPY19L2/FAM209-associated proteins to mediate acrosome anchoring to the nuclear envelope. Therefore, these findings established a sequential DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein–Arp complex–CAPZA3 scaffold extending from the nuclear envelope to the acrosome that is indispensable for fertilization. Collectively, we defined a previously unidentified structural and molecular framework for fertilization and provided insights into the diagnosis and treatment of fertilization failure.

title: METTL3-mediated m6A modification of DNMT1 enhances ovarian cancer progression
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC), the most lethal subtype of ovarian cancer, is often diagnosed at advanced stages and remains associated with poor clinical outcome. In this study, we identify a critical oncogenic role of the RNA methyltransferase METTL3 and the
                    N
                    6
                    -methyladenosine (m
                    6
                    A) RNA modification pathway in HGSOC. Suppression of METTL3, either genetically or pharmacologically, and depletion of its binding partner METTL14 impair ovarian cancer proliferation and tumor progression. Mechanistically, we show that METTL3-mediated m
                    6
                    A deposition enhances the translation of DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1), the primary maintenance DNA methyltransferase responsible for preserving genome-wide methylation patterns and silencing tumor suppressor genes. Pharmacological inhibition of DNMT1 induces widespread DNA hypomethylation and up-regulation of the tumor suppressors TNFAIP3 and FBXO32. Consistently, METTL3 suppression reduces DNMT1 abundance and derepresses TNFAIP3 and FBXO32 expression. Knockdown and rescue studies further reveal that DNMT1 primarily mediates METTL3-dependent regulation of cell migration, whereas the antiproliferative effects of METTL3 suppression are likely driven by additional downstream targets. Collectively, these findings identify the m
                    6
                    A-METTL3-DNMT1 axis as a mechanistic link between RNA and DNA methylation pathways and a potential therapeutic vulnerability in HGSOC.

title: Persistent bistability of Nordic Seas overflow waters over 800,000 years
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: The stability of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a major uncertainty in projections of future climate. However, direct evidence for AMOC tipping behavior on orbital timescales remains scarce. Here, we reconstruct the strength of Iceland-Scotland Overflow Water, a key lower branch of the deep Atlantic circulation, over the past 800,000 years by combining 12 current-speed records from North Atlantic sediment cores with a data-driven hybrid model. The resulting reconstruction reveals persistent alternation between weak (glacial) and strong (interglacial) circulation modes, pervasive millennial-scale variability within both regimes, and systematic asymmetry between weak-to-strong recoveries and strong-to-weak collapses. Threshold and phase-space analyses show that regime shifts occur within a narrow window of atmospheric carbon dioxide and sea level and often follow hysteresis-like loops. Although bistability persists throughout the last 800,000 years, its sensitivity and timing evolve through time. These findings provide long-term, high-resolution, data-driven constraints on the bistability of Nordic Seas overflow waters and its implications for AMOC resilience in a warming world.

title: Guest Transition Metals in Host Keplerate Nanocapsules as Supramolecular Inorganic Functional Mimics of Monooxygenase Enzymes
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Advanced design of supramolecules can mimic enzyme complexes. Methane monooxygenases have several subparts, hydroxylases active for alkane oxidation, and complexes and channels that regulate electron, proton, substrate, and product access to the active site. The replication of a hydroxylase active site with inclusion of regulatory functionalities within a porous Keplerate nanocapsule host was undertaken. A Cu active site guest within a Keplerate cavity was prepared by an assembly reaction using a histidine surrogate as binding site for Cu II . The guest–host assembly enables transfer of protons and electrons and enables substrate and product diffusion to and from an active site into confined space. Characterization of the guest–host complex was by NMR, XPS, infrared, and Raman spectroscopies. Cyclic voltammetry was used to identify possible hydroxylase reactivity, followed by controlled potential electrolysis to verify hydrocarbon oxygenation. Substrate scope, optimal cathodic potential, and the number of metal sites needed were surveyed. Comparison of substrate reactivity revealed that their access to the active site was rate determining. Kinetics of a “dummy” substrate and product diffusion was measured by Guest Exchange Saturation Transfer 19 F NMR. These guest–host Keplerate nanocapsules represent an initial foray into the mimicking of a complicated metalloenzyme complex in an inorganic synthetic system.

title: Mechanistic Insights Into the Solid‐State Redox Reactions: Role of Organic Piezoelectric Materials
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Mechanochemistry has gained tremendous recent attention because it combines sustainability with the ability to access unique reaction pathways and materials while offering practical advantages for efficient and scalable chemical synthesis. However, predicting solid‐state transformations from mechanical energy remains a formidable challenge, as the current mechanistic models are insufficient. While solid‐state electrocatalytic reactions in the presence of inorganic piezoelectric materials have been demonstrated recently, the ability of piezoelectric organic solids, which possess an order of magnitude lower piezoelectric coefficients, remain completely unexplored. Here, using different crystalline forms, we demonstrate that under ball‐milling, non‐centrosymmetric organic crystals generate piezoelectric potentials that are sufficient to drive a range of redox bond‐forming reactions, including C─B, C─S, C─Se, C─C, and C─P couplings. To further evaluate the role of piezoelectricity, we compared chemically identical crystal forms of a compound, differing only in symmetry: Non‐centrosymmetric crystals are highly reactive, whereas centrosymmetric counterparts remain largely inert. These findings reveal crystal symmetry as a previously unrecognized determinant of chemical function and identify organic piezoelectric solids as active energy‐transduction media for chemical synthesis. More broadly, this work provides a framework for designing self‐powered chemical systems that directly couple mechanical energy harvesting with molecular transformation.

title: Fluorinated Fullerene Derivatives for Thermally Stable Perovskite Solar Cells
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT PCBM (phenyl‐C 61 ‐butyric acid methyl ester) is one of the most used electron transport layers (ETLs) in perovskite solar cells (PSCs). However, PCBM tends to self‐aggregate during the thermal aging process, disrupting film continuity and limiting device lifetime. To address this issue, we synthesized new fluorinated phenyl fullerene derivatives, FPCPB and 5FPCPB, forming a composite fullerene ETL by blending with PCBM. We found that fullerene self‐aggregation was suppressed through the synergistic effects of weak interactions, such as π–π conjugation between phenyl and fluorophenyl groups and C─H···F van der Waals interactions, and the constrained molecular conformation induced by intermolecular steric hindrance, thereby markedly improving film uniformity and thermal stability, reducing defect‐state density, and suppressing ion migration. In addition, the energy level alignment between perovskite and ETL is optimized, enhancing electron transport. Ultimately, 5FPCPB, having more compatible energy levels and stronger conjugation effects than FPCPB, achieved a 26.42% power conversion efficiency (PCE), with improved operational and thermal stability (T 90 under light = 1200 h; T 95 under 85°C > 700 h). The fullerene co‐doping strategy opens a new pathway for achieving high‐performance and thermally stable perovskite devices.

title: π‐Extended Bisallyls Through Valence Isomerism: From Transient Diradicals to Persistent Anions
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Bisallyl diradicals are central intermediates in allene dimerization, yet they are normally too short‐lived to observe under thermal conditions. Here, π‐extension of Staudinger‐type allene dimers weakens the central cyclobutane bond sufficiently to make reversible ring opening accessible near room temperature. Variable‐temperature NMR spectroscopy and ROESY exchange correlations reveal repeated cleavage and reformation of this bond, with activation free energies of 15.77 and 13.79 kcal mol −1 for the Staudinger dimer and its π‐expanded analogue, respectively. Calculations reproduce this trend and identify low‐population open‐shell singlet bisallyls as the intermediates, while explaining the absence of neutral‐state EPR signals. Reduction reverses the relative stability of the closed and open valence isomers. Voltammetry and chemical reduction support a sequence of ring‐opened radical‐anion, dianion, and tetraanion states. The dianion is characterized by NMR spectroscopy and x‐ray diffraction, while spectroscopy and calculations reveal progressive bond redistribution from mixed‐valence allyl‐radical/allyl‐anion character to two allyl‐anion units and, finally, four fluorenyl‐anion‐like termini. These results connect hidden neutral diradicals with persistent reduced bisallyl frameworks through charge‐controlled covalent‐bond reorganization.

title: Boron‐Oxygen Covalent Fusion Enables Narrowband Deep‐Red CP‐OLEDs Based on BODIPY Emitters
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Realizing solution‐processable deep‐red circularly polarized organic light‐emitting diodes (CP‐OLEDs) with both intense CP and high color purity remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report the first solution‐processed narrowband deep‐red circularly polarized hyperfluorescence OLEDs based on a helically chiral boron‐dipyrromethene emitter. Intramolecular boron–oxygen (B–O) covalent fusion simultaneously regulates molecular conjugation and conformational rigidity, thereby suppressing excited‐state structural relaxation and vibronic coupling while preserving efficient deep‐red emission. As a result, BDP‐BO exhibits deep‐red emission at 654 nm with a high photoluminescence quantum yield of 71% and an ultranarrow emission bandwidth of 34 nm (0.10 eV). The corresponding P ‐ and M ‐enantiomers display excellent chiroptical activity, with a luminescence dissymmetry factor (| g lum |) up to 3.54 × 10 −3 and a circularly polarized luminescence brightness ( B CPL ) of 49 M −1 cm −1 . Exploiting these merits, the M ‐ BDP‐BO ‐based device delivers deep‐red electroluminescence (EL) within the National Television System Committee color gamut, a maximum external quantum efficiency of 2.6%, and a large EL dissymmetry factor (| g EL |) of 5.49 × 10 −3 . This work establishes B–O covalent fusion as an effective strategy for simultaneously regulating molecular conjugation and conformational rigidity, providing a versatile platform for high‐performance solution‐processed deep‐red CP‐OLEDs.

title: Porphyrin Integration Enhances Bipolar Redox Accessibility for High‐Rate Sodium‐Based Dual‐Ion Storage
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Closing the gap between theoretical multielectron capacity and practical accessibility remains the central bottleneck for high‐energy organic batteries. Herein, we report a molecular design strategy that integrates a porphyrin motif into a sulfur‐rich conjugated polymer (BTTP) to align electronic structure, state‐dependent ion interactions, and electrochemical kinetics across the bipolar window. Despite possessing a lower theoretical capacity than its reference counterpart (BTB), BTTP achieves an exceptional theoretical capacity utilization of 94.2% (delivering 477 mAh g −1 at 0.5 A g −1 , compared to only 53.5% and 351 mAh g −1 for BTB). Electrokinetic analyses, including GITT and DRT, confirm accelerated apparent ion diffusion and reduced polarization limitations, enabling BTTP to retain 166 mAh g −1 at an ultrahigh current density of 20 A g −1 over 25 000 cycles. Operando/ex situ spectroscopy and theoretical calculations elucidate that the dual pyrrolic/imino nitrogen sites in porphyrin and the sulfur‐rich backbone cooperatively provide potential‐dependent coordination environments for PF 6 − anions and Na + cations. This work suggests that molecular regulation of complementary ion‐interaction environments within multi‐active‐unit frameworks, rather than simply increasing the number of redox units, is important for enhancing rate capability and capacity utilization.

title: Relay Catalysis on Phase‐Separated Janus–CuCo Alloys for Efficient Electrochemical Nitrate Reduction at Industrial Low Concentration
abstract: ABSTRACT Earth‐abundant Cu and Co are attractive electrocatalysts for nitrate reduction to ammonia (NO 3 − RR); however, conventional solid‐solution alloys with single‐phase active sites lack effective intermediate spillover, impeding the hydrogenation of multiple reaction intermediates and limiting NH 3 selectivity under dilute nitrate conditions. Here we report phase‐separated yet electronically coupled Janus–CuCo alloys synthesized via a time–charge regulated electrochemical reduction strategy, forming metallic Cu/Co domains with a well‐defined interphase electronic structure. This Janus architecture enables relay catalysis, in which Cu domains activate NO 3 − , intermediates migrate to Cu−Co interfaces for hydrogenation, and adjacent Co domains promote subsequent NH 3 formation. In situ characterizations reveal pronounced Cu–Co synergy, where Co sites regulate *H‐mediated hydrogenation while the balanced surface coverage of *H and *NO 3 − optimizes NH 3 selectivity and yield. Consequently, the optimized Janus Cu−Co catalyst, Janus–Cu 70 Co 30 /NOMC, achieves a peak NH 3 Faradaic efficiency (FE NH3 ) of 95.5% at −500 mA cm −2 and delivers a FE NH3 of 93.1% with an NH 3 yield rate of 4.2 mg h −1 mg cat −1 at −0.4 V vs RHE in an MEA flow cell under low nitrate concentrations. These findings establish phase separation with electronic coupling, enabled by electrochemical time–charge control, as an effective design principle for efficient multistep NO 3 − RR electrocatalysis.

title: Decoupling Oxygen Reduction From Hydrogen Oxidation on Platinum via Phosphorus Coordination for Reversal‐Tolerant and Durable PEM Fuel Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT During the start‐up/shut‐down (SU/SD) processes of proton‐exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), anode reversal generates an excessively high voltage that accelerates corrosion of the cathode Pt/C catalyst. Conventional approaches focus on blocking the delivery of oxygen or electrons to the anode, but fail to address the intrinsic activity coupling of Pt/C for both hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR) and oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). Here, we report a strategy that can selectively tailor the catalytic function of Pt nanoparticles. We used phosphorus to modulate the electronic structure of low‐loading Pt clusters on a carbon support, forming a Pt/P‐BP catalyst. The P‐coordination downshifts the d ‐band center of Pt cluster, as evidenced by in situ ATR‑FTIR spectroscopy and DFT calculations, thereby widening the activity gap between HOR and ORR. Specifically, compared to Pt/C, Pt/P‐BP enhances HOR mass activity by fivefold while substantially suppressing ORR, transforming Pt from a bifunctional catalyst into a highly selective HOR catalyst. Consequently, Pt/P‐BP achieves a 10.8‐fold higher HOR/ORR selectivity than Pt/C. In SU/SD experiments, the Pt/P‐BP anode significantly reduces carbon corrosion of the cathode catalyst layer, maintaining the fuel cell performance better than Pt/C. This work paves a new avenue toward durable PEMFCs and inspires the selectivity design for electrocatalysts.

title: Atmosphere‐Dependent Encapsulation and Dewetting in Au/ZnO: A Transient‐Overlayer Strategy for Maximizing Metal‐Support Interfacial Catalysis
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT The strong metal–support interaction (SMSI) has traditionally been viewed as a static phenomenon that modulates catalysis through site blocking. Here, we challenge this classical view by demonstrating that SMSI in Au/ZnO is an atmosphere‐dependent dynamic process that can be harnessed to engineer catalytic interfaces. Using in situ transmission electron microscopy, infrared spectroscopy, and X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy, we track the structural evolution of the Au/ZnO interface throughout redox cycles and reaction conditions. Under H 2 , oxygen vacancy formation triggers ZnO x encapsulation, followed by AuZn alloying at elevated temperature, which induces nanoparticle reconstruction and expands the metal‐support interfacial area. Upon exposure to O 2 , the alloy decomposes, and the ZnO x overlayer dewets into nanoislands, with some regions undergoing complete retraction. Under CO oxidation conditions, the fully encapsulated state is lost, yet the H 2 ‐pretreated catalyst exhibits superior activity and stability. This enhancement arises from alloying‐induced interface reconstruction together with residual ZnO nanoislands that persist after dewetting, creating an enlarged and highly active metal–oxide interface. Our work demonstrates a transient‐overlayer strategy for catalyst design, in which a pre‐formed SMSI layer serves as a precursor that, through controlled redox cycling or reaction conditions, transforms into a high‐interface area, sintering‐resistant catalytic architecture, thereby transcending the classical encapsulation‐activity dilemma.

title: Structure‐Guided Design of Pepper‐Binding Fluorophores Through Hydrogen‐Bonding Engineering
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Pepper fluorescent RNAs (FRs) enable spatiotemporal imaging of intracellular RNA with high resolution. Although spectral optimization of the HBC scaffold has extended coverage from cyan to red, systematic refinement of binding affinity, photostability, and brightness remains largely unexplored. We describe a hydrogen‐bonding strategy that strengthens fluorophore‐aptamer interactions by incorporating hydroxyl groups or polyethylene glycol (PEG) moieties into HBC derivatives. The resulting compounds, MBC and PBC620, bind Pepper over 6‐fold and 10‐fold more tightly than their parent dyes HBC and HBC620, respectively, and exhibit correspondingly higher signal‐to‐noise ratios and enhanced photostability, with 2.1‐fold and 1.5‐fold increases in cellular brightness. Molecular models reveal that improved affinity stems from optimally positioned hydrogen bonds with RNA nucleotides. MBC enables real‐time tracking of genomic loci with enhanced contrast compared to standard HBC. This work establishes structure‐guided interface engineering as a general strategy for improving fluorescent RNA systems.

title: Resurrecting Robust CYP152 Peroxygenases for Versatile Biocatalysis
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Cytochrome P450 CYP152s are attractive biocatalysts which catalyze decarboxylation and hydroxylation of fatty acids using H 2 O 2 as a co‐substrate (peroxygenase activity). Contemporary CYP152s have limited stability and substrate scope. Here we characterized eight reconstructed variants of CYP152 obtained using ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR). The results showed that variants remote from Jeotgalicoccus sp. 8456 (CYP152L1) in the tree used for the ASR tended to catalyze hydroxylation, while nodes closer to CYP152L1 favored decarboxylation; this transition correlates with Q85H substitution and FG‐loop insertion alongside other structural features. Three reconstructed variants exhibit high T m (66°C–76°C), tolerance to solvents, H 2 O 2 , extreme pH, and use non‐native substrates. CYP152‐AncG2 can catalyze one‐pot chemoenzymatic C─C bond coupling reactions to synthesize methoxy stilbene and can serve as a template for directed evolution. X‐ray structure at 1.83 Å and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations indicate that loop structures, surface salt bridges, and optimized access tunnels in CYP152‐AncG2 are key for enabling its superior features. These findings provide insights into the structural and evolutionary features of robust peroxygenase templates for expanding peroxygenase biocatalysis.

title: Aptamers enable a distinct mode of conformational DNA recognition
abstract:
Abstract
                  Watson–Crick base-pairing defines the classical paradigm of nucleic-acid interactions, but growing research reveals noncanonical modes beyond this framework. Here we uncover a mode of interactions by which two DNA strands associate through a ligand-induced conformational rearrangement. Upon binding a small molecule, a structure-switching primary aptamer folds into a conformation that exposes a previously inaccessible docking interface. An independently evolved secondary aptamer recognizes this interface primarily through noncanonical interactions rather than sequence complementarity, reporting the ligand-bound state of the primary aptamer. This interaction is conformation-sensitive: single base-pair changes in the primary aptamer modulate secondary aptamer recognition. Across four chemically distinct small-molecule targets—serotonin, dopamine, testosterone and deoxycorticosterone 21-glucoside—secondary aptamers were identified for three, and the serotonin system was translated into surface-based sandwich assays. These results demonstrate that a ligand-induced conformational state, rather than sequence complementarity or the chemical identity of the ligand, can serve as the epitope for nucleic-acid recognition, expanding the molecular features that DNA can be evolved to detect.

title: Low-Solvent Mechanochemical MOF Carrier Nanoarchitectonics for Targeted Quercetin Delivery for Dual-Mode ROS and Anti-inflammation Protection against LPS-Induced Acute Lung Injury
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Nowadays, inhalable administration of nanomedicines is an appealing concept for acute lung injury (ALI). For ALI nanomedicine, it is appealing to achieve targeted delivery and on-demand release in the ALI microenvironment, which is acidic, rich in reactive oxygen species (ROS), and with elevated inflammatory mediator levels. Notably, customized metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) could fulfill these requirements and thus are promising nanocarriers for ALI medicine delivery, but MOFs formulated often suffer from unreacted residues with hazardous risk. Herein, we report a low-solvent mechanochemical synthesis method to formulate cerium-doped zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (Ce-ZIFs) stabilized by Pluronic F127 as drug delivery nanocarriers to load quercetin for targeted preventive ALI therapy. The nanoplatform exhibits robust structural integrity, high drug loading capacity, excellent biocompatibility, and pH-responsive release of quercetin under acidic conditions, mimicking the inflamed lung microenvironment. Importantly, the nanoplatform ameliorates pro-inflammatory mediators (TNF-α, IL-6), inhibits pulmonary edema, and attenuates alveolar injury in an LPS-induced ALI mouse model. Notably, Ce/ZIF promotes the Ce+3/Ce+4 redox process to generate catalase-like activity for catalytic reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging and sustainable antioxidant properties. Transcriptome sequencing and biological validation also revealed that the nanoplatform showed its remarkable ability to counteract LPS-induced oxidative damage and inflammatory responses by suppressing Th1 cell polarization. This work demonstrates a Ce/ZIF platform formulated using a scalable, low-solvent mechanochemical synthesis method, presenting a biocompatible MOF platform with significant promise for targeted pulmonary delivery with protective potential against LPS-induced acute lung injury.

title: Engineered Dielectric Response of Liquid-Filled Interfacial Bubbles in van der Waals Heterostructures
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Interfacial bubbles in van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures are typically regarded as unavoidable byproducts of stacking. Here, we show that they can be repurposed as engineered dielectric nanocavities by intentionally trapping selected liquids during assembly. A simple prewetting step before stamp transfer forms liquid-filled bubbles at hBN/graphite interfaces containing acetone, ethanol, H2O, and NaCl(aq), alongside untreated reference bubbles. Electrostatic force microscopy (EFM), crosstalk correction, and finite-element modeling enable quantitative extraction of the effective dielectric constant (εeff) of individual bubbles, revealing higher εeff for all liquid-filled bubbles than for untreated ones. To estimate the apparent core permittivity of the confined contents, each bubble is modeled as a liquid core enclosed by an hBN shell. Simulations of the tip–bubble–substrate geometry yield core dielectric constants (εcore) larger than εeff yet physically consistent with the trapped media. Acetone and ethanol exhibit εcore values close to their expected dielectric properties, whereas water shows a reduced εcore consistent with nanoconfined pure water. Notably, NaCl(aq) shows a larger εcore than pure water, suggesting distinct electrolyte dielectric behavior under nanoscale confinement. This work establishes vdW bubbles as versatile platforms for engineering local electrostatic functionality and probing confined-liquid dielectric physics in two-dimensional (2D) material assemblies.

title: Stress‐Regulated Li Plating in Hybrid Ag–Carbon/Carbon Nanofiber Anodes for Durable All‐Solid‐State Batteries
abstract: ABSTRACT All‐solid‐state batteries (ASSBs) with Li‐metal or Li‐metal‐free anodes enable high energy density, yet high‐loading cathodes induce severe mechanical instability, leading to rapid cell failure. Herein, we identify stress accumulation caused by repetitive Li plating/stripping as a critical degradation origin in ASSBs and propose a mechanically adaptive Ag–carbon/carbon nanofiber (CNF) hybrid anode to address this challenge. Operando pressure analysis and mechanical modeling reveal that increasing cathode areal capacity substantially amplifies pressure fluctuations and dynamic mechanical instability, leading to interfacial disruption and short‐circuiting. To mitigate this behavior, the Ag–C interlayer and porous CNF framework were independently customized to provide complementary electrochemical regulation and mechanical buffering functions. The Ag–C layer promotes uniform Li nucleation through Ag–Li alloy‐assisted interfacial regulation, while the porous CNF host accommodates volumetric changes and dissipates stress. Phase‐field modeling and microstructural analyses reveal sequential Ag–Li alloying within the Ag–C interlayer, CNF lithiation and pore filling, and controlled interfacial Li deposition, thereby spatially redistributing volumetric expansion. Consequently, the Ag–C/CNF architecture significantly reduces pressure fluctuation and enables stable cycling over 250 cycles under high‐loading conditions (∼5 mAh cm −2 ). Furthermore, stable pouch‐cell operation is demonstrated under practical stack pressures of 1 and 2 MPa, highlighting a viable strategy for mechanically robust high‐energy‐density ASSBs.

title: Super‐Toughness Self‐Healing Composite Solid Electrolyte With Structured Interfacial Reconstruction Enabling Fast Ion Transport and Stable Interface for High‐Performance Solid‐State Lithium Metal Batteries
abstract: ABSTRACT Lithium–metal batteries are widely regarded as a key direction for next‐generation energy storage systems due to high energy density. However, LiNi 0 . 8 Co 0 . 1 Mn 0 . 1 O 2 ||Li battery systems face severe challenges in practical application, including lithium dendrite growth, interfacial side reactions and structural degradation of high‐nickel cathodes. Here, we proposed a versatile modification strategy combining in‐situ interfacial transformation with polymer phase regulation to fabricate self‐healing solid polymer electrolyte with fast ion transport and stable interface. This strategy not only constructs fast ion channels and suppresses hydrofluoric acid production by in‐situ converting Li 2 CO 3 on the Li 6.4 La 3 Zr 1.4 Ta 0.6 O 12 surface into Li 2 PO 3 F interfacial layer, but also induces the transition of PVDF from α‐phase to high polarity β‐phase using ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid to promote lithium salt dissolution and reduce Li + migration resistance. The as‐prepared electrolyte exhibits extended electrochemical voltage windows (5.13 V), high room‐temperature ionic conductivity (1.694 mS cm − 1 ), excellent thermal stability (200°C), high elongation at break (422.6%), and superior cycling stability (89.4% retention after 500 cycles at 1 C). A non‐destructive monitoring method based on d p /|d Q | and d T /|d Q | differential signals has been developed to track electrochemical‐mechanical‐thermal responses during battery operation. This work provides an effective strategy for designing solid polymer electrolytes with high ionic conductivity and interfacial stability.

title: Synergistic Anion Regulation Inducing Fluoride‐Rich SEI and Defect‐Rich MnO 2 for Stable Dual Electrode‐Free Zn‐MnO 2 Batteries
abstract: ABSTRACT Dual electrode‐free (DEF) Zn─MnO 2 batteries based on dissolution‐deposition chemistry are promising candidates for large‐scale energy storage due to their lightweight architecture and high theoretical capacity (616 mAh g −1 ). However, poor interfacial reversibility and the accumulation of “dead manganese” significantly limit their lifespan. Here, we demonstrate a stable DEF battery enabled by an anion‐regulation strategy using a hybrid electrolyte (E‐OA) comprising trifluoromethanesulfonate (OTf − ) and acetate (Ac − ) ions. At the anode, OTf − facilitates the formation of a fluoride‐rich solid–electrolyte interphase (SEI), effectively suppressing dendrite growth and the hydrogen evolution reaction. At the cathode, the synergistic anionic environment elevates the MnO 2 nucleation overpotential, shifting the electrocrystallization pathway to an instantaneous nucleation mode. The kinetically driven growth process traps abundant structural defects, identified as proton‐compensated manganese vacancies (Ruetschi defects). These vacancies lower the thermodynamic energy barrier for Mn─O bond cleavage, thereby ensuring highly reversible dissolution. Consequently, the E‐OA‐based DEF battery achieves exceptional stability for over 7500 cycles at 0.5 mAh cm −2 and sustains 600 cycles at 2 mAh cm −2 (10 mA cm −2 ), demonstrating superior rate capability and versatility in both flow and gel battery configurations. This work provides a transformative strategy for high‐energy aqueous batteries via tailored anion chemistry and kinetics‐driven defect engineering.

title: Polar crystals as catalytic platforms for solar energy conversion
abstract: Polar crystals possess non-centrosymmetric structures that generate spontaneous polarization and a built-in electric field, enabling efficient charge separation. This Review discusses their use as catalysts for converting solar energy into chemical energy, covering the advantages of polar single crystals, multilevel polarization engineering, key challenges and future directions.

title: Cold Atmospheric Plasma–Enabled SiO x Nanocoatings for Surface Energy Modulation and Enhanced Seed Germination
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Modern agricultural systems demand higher and more reliable yields under increasing constraints on land, water, and fertilizer inputs. Rapid and uniform seed germination is therefore critical for improving crop establishment and overall yield performance. Although existing strategies, such as ionizing gas treatments, polymer coatings, and nanoparticle-based seed treatments, can enhance water uptake and early vigor, they often suffer from limited stability, processing complexity, or potential seed damage. Here, we introduce a dry, cold atmospheric plasma (CAP)-assisted deposition platform for the conformal SiOx nanocoating of seeds, enabling a hydrophilic, storage-stable surface modification under ambient conditions. The deposition process was systematically optimized to achieve rapid, uniform coating formation directly on the seed surface. As a model system, corn seeds (Zea mays L.) were coated with SiOx nanofilms under optimized conditions. Wettability analysis revealed a ∼4-fold reduction in the static water contact angle for SiOx-coated seeds relative to pristine controls, compared with a ∼2.9-fold reduction for plasma-treated seeds without precursor introduction. Importantly, the SiOx-induced hydrophilicity exhibited superior stability, showing less than 3° contact angle recovery after 21 days of storage, whereas plasma-treated seeds alone displayed ∼50° recovery within 120 h. This stable and enhanced surface hydrophilicity translated into accelerated germination and improved early seedling vigor, resulting in SiOx-coated seeds exhibiting improved total seedling growth immediately after treatment and maintaining an approximately 38% increase compared with pristine controls after storage, demonstrating consistent storage stability. In comparison, the early-germination and seedling-growth advantages of plasma-treated seeds diminished substantially after storage, indicating that CAP-deposited SiOx provides a more persistent and storage-stable functional modification. Collectively, these results establish CAP-deposited SiOx nanocoatings as a scalable, solvent-free nanotechnology platform for stabilizing seed hydrophilicity, accelerating germination, and promoting early seedling growth under agronomically relevant conditions.

title: Controlling Compensation Doping via Multivalent Platinum Acceptors in Tantalum Oxide Thin Films
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Heterostructures of platinum (Pt) and tantalum oxide (Ta2O5) find widespread use in electronic and energy-conversion device applications, yet the electronic role of Pt incorporated within Ta2O5 remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the influence of Pt incorporation on the electronic structure and properties of amorphous Ta2O5 using two precisely controlled ternary atomic layer deposition (ALD) pathways. Oxygen plasma-enhanced deposition produces host matrices with significantly lower native defect and impurity concentrations than conventional thermal water-based ALD, enabling a systematic investigation of the interplay between Pt dopants and native defects. Controlled Pt incorporation over the range of 0.9–1.9 atom % yields homogeneous, amorphous Pt-doped Ta2O5 thin films containing exclusively Pt(II) and Pt(IV) oxidation states, with no evidence of metallic Pt formation. While the optical bandgap of the Ta2O5 host matrix remains largely unchanged, Pt incorporation introduces optically active acceptor states near the valence band maximum, increases sub-bandgap absorption, and shifts the Fermi level toward the midgap. The relative Pt(II)/Pt(IV) population depends strongly on the defect landscape of the host matrix and exhibits a linear dependence on the Fermi level position, demonstrating Fermi level-controlled charge compensation between native donor defects and multivalent Pt acceptor states. Density functional theory corroborates the acceptor character of Pt and assigns the introduced states primarily to Pt 5d orbitals. Experimentally constructed band diagrams and charge transport measurements further show that Pt incorporation provides a direct means of tuning the electronic properties of Ta2O5. These results demonstrate that multivalent Pt doping serves as a controllable strategy for engineering the electronic structure and transport characteristics of functional Ta2O5 thin films, with direct relevance to memristive, dielectric, and photoelectrochemical devices.

title: Decoupling Electrochemical Performance from External Pressure via Mechanically Interlocked 3D Interfaces for Ultra-low-pressure Supercapacitor Pouch Cells
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Supercapacitor pouch cells typically require substantial external stack pressure (typically >2 MPa) to maintain intimate internal interface contact. However, the heavy packaging modules introduce significant inactive mass, reducing system-level energy density. Herein, we report a two-step aligned 3D imprinting strategy that fundamentally decouples electrochemical performance from external compression. By engineering a mechanically interlocked structure, the compaction force is precisely directed toward the interfaces between the active particles, as well as between the particles and the current collector. This prevents lateral slippage, achieving ultra-low internal electrode resistance and conformal interface contact. Consequently, compared with planar electrodes, imprinted electrodes exhibit a 14.3-fold lower interfacial resistance and a 2.7-fold lower equivalent series resistance even under 0.3 MPa stack pressure, delivering an unprecedented average power density of 285 kW kg–1 at 1 mg cm–2 and 28.4 kW kg–1 at 5 mg cm–2. Notably, pouch cells based on 3D-D electrodes sustain 100,000 cycles with 99% capacitance retention, benefiting from the mechanically stabilized interface and the suppressed resistance evolution. Furthermore, this paradigm is compatible with roll-to-roll manufacturing processes, providing a versatile and scalable approach for the next generation of high-power, lightweight, and ultra-low-pressure supercapacitor systems.

title: Carboxylic Acid-Based Hole Transport Layer with Both Anchoring and Passivation in Inverted Perovskite Solar Cells
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The hole transport layer (HTL) plays a pivotal role in the performance of inverted perovskite solar cells (PSCs), especially in carrier transport, anchoring to the substrate as a buried interface, and defect passivation. Novel HTLs that simultaneously achieve indium tin oxide (ITO) substrate anchoring, passivation of buried perovskite defects, and favorable interfacial energy alignment are seldom addressed. In this work, we designed a novel HTL (denoted as TPCOOH), which is functionalized with dicarboxylic acid groups in the central phenyl ring, which can anchor onto ITO substrates and passivate the top perovskite, as well as coupling with methylthio-substituted triphenylamine and thiophene units to generate suitable energy alignment and transfer the hole, realizing both passivation and anchoring effects. TPHex, as a control, had dihexyl substitution in the center. Inverted PSC devices based on TPCOOH and TPHex as hole transport layers (0.1 cm2) achieved power conversion efficiencies of 24.68% and 23.72%, respectively. The improved efficiency of TPCOOH-based devices is attributed to suppressed nonradiative recombination, rapid interfacial charge transfer, and minimal energy loss due to well-matched energy levels. These improvements are ascribed to the carboxyl groups in TPCOOH, which anchor to ITO, thus ensuring better film coverage and improved charge transport, while the passivation functionality simultaneously mitigates perovskite defects. Notably, the TPCOOH and TPHex devices retain 75% and 65% of their initial power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) after 1200 h of thermal aging at 65 ± 5 °C in a nitrogen atmosphere.

title: Unlocking Wide‐Temperature Battery States via Noninvasive Nonlinear Ultrasound
abstract: ABSTRACT Lithium‐ion batteries (LIBs) are central to modern energy storage, yet evaluating their internal states under extreme thermal fluctuations remains a critical challenge. Here we present a non‐destructive evaluation framework that leverages the quasi‐static component (QSC) of nonlinear ultrasonic guided waves. By integrating an operando electro‐acoustic‐thermal platform, we isolate temperature‐induced artefacts from intrinsic acoustic signals. This statistical compensation enables the precise, simultaneous prediction of state of charge (SOC) and state of charge relative to nominal capacity (SOC N ) across a wide temperature span (−10°C to 40°C). Furthermore, in situ multidimensional characterization maps these ultrasonic signatures to temperature‐dependent mechanics and irreversible capacity fade mechanisms. Ultimately, this unified framework provides a scalable, quantitative diagnostic tool for reliable energy systems operating under extreme environments.

title: Rethinking Battery Safety: Unveiling Aluminum Propellant‐Like Reactions During Thermal Runaway and Developing Protective Solutions
abstract: ABSTRACT Battery safety remains a critical challenge in the large‐scale deployment of lithium‐ion batteries. While thermal runaway is typically attributed to exothermic reactions involving electrode materials and electrolytes, the contribution of current collectors has been largely overlooked. Here, we demonstrate that the conventionally presumed inert aluminum (Al) current collector engages in intense exothermic reactions with various cathode materials at temperatures exceeding 600°C. This reactivity is catalyzed by fluorides, which disrupt the Al passivation layer, resembling combustion mechanisms observed in Al‐based rocket propellants. The specific heat release from Al oxidation (−22 to −33 kJ g −1 ) is nearly twice that of the electrolyte (−12 to −16 kJ g −1 ). Considering that the Al mass is approximately half that of the electrolyte, its theoretical thermal contribution during thermal runaway is comparable to that of the electrolyte. Employing fluorine‐free electrolytes can suppress the propellant‐like reaction. Together with flame‐retardant strategies, the total heat release during thermal runaway can be further reduced, with the measured peak temperatures around pouch cells being effectively suppressed below 400°C. This work uncovers a pervasive yet previously underappreciated high‐energy reaction in batteries and offers new design strategies for improving thermal safety.

title: Spatial‐Decoupled Synergy between Asymmetric Ni‐N 3 Sites and Ni Nanoparticles Extending the Air‐Tolerant Poisoning Limit of MgH 2 Hydrogen Storage
abstract: ABSTRACT Solid‐state MgH 2 holds immense promise for high‐capacity hydrogen storage, yet its practical deployment is severely hindered by extreme atmospheric susceptibility and an elusive activated dehydrogenation mechanism. Herein, we report a armor like architectural design featuring asymmetric Ni‐N 3 sites and nanoparticles (NPs) co‐decorated within a flexible nitrogen‐doped graphene (NG). Driven by the electronic synergy between the Ni‐N 3 sites and the highly active Ni NPs, the NG achieves robust encapsulation of MgH 2 , providing a rigid size‐exclusion barrier against ambient O 2 /H 2 O infiltration. Concurrently, strong electronic interactions between MgH 2 and Ni species optimize the MgH 2 electronic structure, which further reduces its reactivity toward O 2 /H 2 O, enabling the MgH 2 to preserve its full capacity even after a 28‐day cumulative air exposure. Furthermore, the encapsulated Ni NPs undergo an in situ reaction to form Mg 2 Ni nanorivets, which serve as high‐flux interfacial hydrogen pumps, while creating a vital spatial buffer during dynamic cycling, thereby achieving 95% capacity retention over 360 cycles at 300°C. Density functional theory calculations confirm that the electronic hybridization induced by the asymmetric Ni‐N 3 sites, Ni NPs, and Mg 2 Ni nanorivets destabilizes Mg‐H bonds. This multi‐scale engineering of environmental isolation, electronic modulation, and structural riveting presents a robust blueprint for air‐tolerant, fast‐kinetics solid‐state hydrogen storage.

title: EGCG@ZIF-8@Polydopamine-Functionalized Janus Nanofibrous Dressing with Directional Exudate Transport and Photothermal Antibacterial Activity for Infected Wound Treatment
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The treatment of infected skin wounds continues to face multiple challenges, including bacterial resistance, persistent inflammation, oxidative damage, and inadequate exudate management. To address these issues, a multifunctional Janus wound dressing was constructed to achieve coordinated infection control and tissue repair. Zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (ZIF-8) was used as a nanocarrier for the natural antioxidant molecule, and polydopamine surface coating endowed the composite nanoparticles with photothermal antibacterial activity. The composite nanoparticles were subsequently incorporated into a hydrophobic polycaprolactone layer by electrospinning and combined with a hydrophilic polyacrylonitrile layer containing a pH indicator, thereby forming a bilayer structure with unidirectional liquid transport, visual monitoring, and wound protection functions. The dressing promotes the outward transfer of wound exudate and produces an observable color response to changes in environmental pH. Under near-infrared irradiation, the antibacterial rate of the dressing reached 98.89% against E. coli and 99.99% against S. aureus. The dressing also possesses excellent free-radical-scavenging capacity, indicating its potential to alleviate excessive oxidative stress in infected wounds. Animal experiments further demonstrated that the dressing reduced the local infection burden, promoted wound closure, collagen deposition, and tissue formation, and caused no obvious histopathological abnormalities in major organs. Overall, this study presents a multifunctional Janus nanofibrous dressing that integrates antibacterial activity, antioxidant function, exudate regulation, and wound-status monitoring, providing a material-design approach for the repair of infected skin wounds.

title: Synergetic Nano-bending, Photo-switching, and Macrocycle Shuttling Effects of Vibration-Induced Emission Lassos on Photoluminescence Properties of Hydrazone-Based [1]Rotaxanes
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract 9,14-Diphenyl-9,14-dihydrodibenzo[a,c]phenazine (DPAC) fluorophores exhibited large Stokes shifts and vibration-induced emission (VIE) with bistable cyan (at 475 nm) and orange (at 600 nm) emissions, whereas hydrazone fluorophores (cyan emission at 475 nm) underwent reversible Z/E photo-isomerization, enabling efficient photo-switching. Herein, we introduced synergetic nano-bending and photo-switchable effects on optical switchable hydrazone linkers and macrocycle shuttling effects of VIE-active DPAC stoppers in [1]rotaxanes, wherein mechanically interlocked architecture-imposed spatial constraints could modulate photoluminescence (PL) behaviors in response to multiple external stimuli. Surprisingly, the highest lifetime τavg1 = 11.8 ns (cyan emission lifetime monitored at 475 nm) was obtained in the loosened lasso owing to stronger intramolecular hydrogen bonds of hydrazone units with minor constraints of nano-bending. While macrocycle shuttling was acid/base-triggered between the loosened lasso with a near-white-light emission [CIE (0.26, 0.32)] and the tightened lasso with an orange emission [CIE (0.37, 0.36)], [1]rotaxanes could tune synergetic PL emissions by modulating bent/planar conformations of DPAC units via acid/base controls and Z/E photo-isomerization of hydrazone units upon 365/450 nm exposures in isopropanol (IPA), respectively. The non-interlocked analogue exhibited the largest lifetime decrease (Δτavg1 = –1.9 ns), whereas the loosened and tightened lassos showed smaller decreases of Δτavg1 = –1.6 and –0.6 ns, respectively, demonstrating that nano-bending constraints suppressed hydrogen-bond disruption during Z/E photo-isomerization. Furthermore, the loosened lasso exhibited temperature- and viscosity-responsive emissions due to hydrogen-bonding disruptions of hydrazone units and progressive planarization of DPAC units upon heating to induce lower viscosity. These results highlight the potential of [1]rotaxanes as stimuli-responsive luminescent molecular systems, enabling proof-of-concept demonstrations in temperature and viscosity sensing as well as optical information encoding.

title: Pain-Perception-Inspired Neuromorphic Sensing: Nonmonotonic Electrical Response and Spatial Visualization in a Near-Infrared-Responsive MXene Hydrogel
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Neuromorphic sensory devices that encode environmental stimuli at the sensing interface offer a route toward more adaptive machine–environment interactions. Ionic hydrogels provide mechanically compliant, ion-conducting hydrated networks that can incorporate photothermal components. However, many near-infrared (NIR)-responsive hydrogels show conductivity changes in one direction, while terminal electrical signals provide little information about stimulus location. Achieving response-direction reversal and spatially resolved visual feedback in one soft material using a single NIR input, therefore, remains challenging. Inspired by protective inhibition and post-stimulus rebound in pain-related neural signaling, we developed an NIR neuromorphic sensory device based on a Ca–PAA–EMB@IL-MXene hydrogel. The material couples photothermal conversion by IL-MXene with temperature-dependent ion transport in a hydrated Ca2+-coordinated PAA-EMB network.
